elements.name: Blue-Green Deployment
elements.what: Two identical production environments are maintained and releases go live by switching traffic from the active (blue) to the newly deployed (green) environment.
elements.problem: Releasing in place risks downtime and slow rollback; keeping a fully deployed standby environment makes cutover and rollback a routing switch instead of a redeploy.
elements.named_in: Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010); also BlueGreenDeployment - Fowler bliki (2010)

elements.name: Canary Release
aka: incremental rollout to a user subset
elements.what: A new version is deployed to a small slice of production servers or users and observed before the rollout is widened to the whole fleet.
elements.problem: Full-fleet releases expose every user to an undetected defect at once; a canary bounds the blast radius and turns release into a monitored experiment.
elements.named_in: Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010); also Site Reliability Engineering - Beyer et al. (2016)

elements.name: Rolling Deployment
elements.what: Instances in a load-balanced pool are replaced with the new version a few at a time, keeping the service up while old and new versions briefly coexist.
elements.problem: Replacing an entire fleet at once requires downtime or double capacity; rolling replacement trades a window of mixed-version operation for zero-downtime upgrades within existing capacity.
elements.named_in: Kubernetes Documentation - Deployments (RollingUpdate strategy) (living)

elements.name: Feature-Flag-Driven Release
elements.what: Code ships to production dark behind runtime toggles, and release becomes a configuration act - enabling the flag for cohorts, rings, or percentages - independent of deployment.
elements.problem: Coupling release to deployment forces long-lived branches and big-bang exposure; runtime toggles let incomplete or risky features ride mainline deploys and be exposed, tested, and killed selectively.
elements.named_in: Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags) - Hodgson (2017); also Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: design realm has feature-flag (the in-code toggle point/router mechanism); this entry is the release-strategy structure built on it. Kept per the same-name rule.

elements.name: Deployment Pipeline
elements.what: An automated, staged structure through which every change flows from commit to production - build, automated test stages, and deployment stages, each gating promotion of the same artifact.
elements.problem: Manual, ad-hoc release paths make delivery slow and unrepeatable; a single automated pipeline makes the route to production an inspectable, versioned system structure.
elements.named_in: Continuous Delivery - Humble & Farley (2010), ch. 5 'Anatomy of the Deployment Pipeline'
elements.borderline: Practice-adjacent (CI/CD is pass-7 territory), but the pipeline itself is a named, recurring structure - stages, gates, artifact promotion - not just a practice; included as the structural core of the CD literature.

elements.name: Load Balancer
aka: server farm behind a virtual IP
elements.what: An intermediary distributes incoming requests across a pool of equivalent service instances, presenting the pool as one logical endpoint.
elements.problem: A single instance limits capacity and is a single point of failure; a fronting distributor lets capacity scale horizontally and routes around dead instances.
elements.named_in: Release It! - Nygard (2007/2018)

elements.name: Scale Cube
aka: X-axis cloning / Y-axis functional decomposition / Z-axis data partitioning
elements.what: A three-axis model of scaling structures: X - cloning identical instances behind a load balancer, Y - splitting by function/service, Z - partitioning by data/customer subset.
elements.problem: Systems that only clone hit data and code-complexity limits; naming the three orthogonal scaling structures lets architects combine duplication, decomposition, and sharding deliberately.
elements.named_in: The Art of Scalability - Abbott & Fisher (2009; 2nd ed. 2015)
elements.borderline: A named model organizing three scaling structures rather than a single mechanism; included because it is the established name for the trio and each axis is a concrete, bridgeable deployment structure (sharding and functional-split design elements bridge to its axes). Verified live at akfpartners.com this session.

elements.name: Auto-Scaling
elements.what: The instance pool grows and shrinks automatically, driven by metrics or schedules evaluated against scaling policies.
elements.problem: Static provisioning wastes capacity at trough and fails at peak; policy-driven elasticity matches deployed capacity to demand without operator action.
elements.named_in: Autoscaling guidance - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (living); also AWS Auto Scaling documentation

elements.name: Immutable Infrastructure
elements.what: Deployed servers/images are never modified in place; every change produces a new image that replaces the old instance wholesale.
elements.problem: In-place patching accumulates configuration drift and snowflake servers; rebuilding from a versioned image makes every environment reproducible and rollback a redeploy of the previous image.
elements.named_in: ImmutableServer - Kief Morris (martinfowler.com bliki, 2013); also Infrastructure as Code - Morris (2016)
elements.borderline: Practice-vs-structure judged: kept because it names a deployment structure (versioned images replacing mutable servers), not merely a working habit; the enclosing infrastructure-as-code practice is rejected below.

elements.name: Deployment Stamps
elements.what: The whole solution is deployed as multiple independent copies (stamps), each serving a defined subset of tenants or a region, with routing in front.
elements.problem: A single shared deployment cannot bound blast radius, tenant isolation, or per-region data residency; replicating the entire stack as units scales by adding stamps and contains failure within one.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (living)

elements.name: Defense in Depth
elements.what: Multiple independent security controls are layered along the path to an asset so that compromising any single control does not compromise the system.
elements.problem: Any single control can fail or be bypassed; stacking heterogeneous barriers forces an attacker to defeat several mechanisms and buys detection time.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006); also NIST SP 800-53 usage

elements.name: Zero Trust Architecture
elements.what: A security architecture in which no implicit trust is granted by network location; every access to a resource is individually authenticated and authorized per session via policy decision/enforcement points.
elements.problem: Perimeter-based models grant broad trust once inside the network, so a single breach yields lateral movement; moving enforcement to each resource access removes the trusted interior.
elements.named_in: Zero Trust Architecture - Rose, Borchert, Mitchell, Connelly (NIST SP 800-207, 2020)

elements.name: Demilitarized Zone
elements.what: Externally reachable services are placed in a separate network segment between two firewall layers, isolating them from both the internet and the internal network.
elements.problem: Public-facing servers are the most exposed components; segregating them means their compromise does not grant direct access to internal systems.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

elements.name: Firewall
elements.what: A choke point on a network boundary that inspects traffic and permits or denies it according to an access policy, at packet, connection, or application level.
elements.problem: Hosts cannot each be trusted to police every peer; concentrating traffic through a policy-enforcing boundary node makes network access control administrable and auditable.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

elements.name: Privilege Separation (process topology)
elements.what: A program is decomposed into a small privileged monitor process and unprivileged worker processes that perform the risky work and request privileged operations over a narrow IPC interface.
elements.problem: A single-process service running with privileges turns any exploited bug into full compromise; splitting across a process boundary confines exploitation to a deprivileged worker.
elements.named_in: Preventing Privilege Escalation - Provos, Friedl & Honeyman (USENIX Security, 2003)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: design realm has privilege-separation (in-program privilege dropping); this entry is the multi-process system topology sense, which Phase 1's security scout parked upward. Kept per the same-name rule.

elements.name: Sandbox
elements.what: Untrusted or exposed code runs inside a confined execution domain whose access to the OS and to other components is restricted to an explicit, minimal interface.
elements.problem: Code that parses hostile input or runs third-party logic will eventually be exploited; structural confinement bounds what an exploited component can reach.
elements.named_in: Efficient Software-Based Fault Isolation - Wahbe, Lucco, Anderson & Graham (SOSP, 1993)

elements.name: Trusted Execution Environment
elements.what: A hardware-isolated execution partition runs security-critical code and holds secrets, exposing only a narrow call interface to the untrusted rich OS beside it.
elements.problem: Keys and critical logic cannot be protected by an OS that may itself be compromised; a hardware-enforced parallel world keeps them safe even under full OS compromise.
elements.named_in: TEE System Architecture - GlobalPlatform (living specification)
elements.borderline: Hardware-adjacent as charter notes, but the split into secure-world and normal-world software with a defined boundary is a software architecture structure, first-class for the corpus's embedded center of gravity.

elements.name: Policy Decision Point / Policy Enforcement Point
elements.what: Authorization is externalized: enforcement points embedded at resource boundaries defer every access decision to a central policy decision point that evaluates declarative policy.
elements.problem: Authorization logic scattered through components is inconsistent and unauditable; separating decision from enforcement centralizes policy while keeping enforcement local to each resource.
elements.named_in: eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML) 3.0 - OASIS Standard (2013); terminology from IETF RFC 2753
elements.borderline: Design realm holds reference-monitor (with PDP/PEP noted in its aka as the operational split); this entry catalogs the distributed authorization topology itself, the sense Phase 1's security scout parked upward.

elements.name: Intrusion Detection System
elements.what: A dedicated component observes network traffic or host activity and flags (or blocks, as IPS) patterns indicating attack or misuse.
elements.problem: Preventive controls fail silently; a separate observing component turns compromise attempts into detectable, alertable events.
elements.named_in: An Intrusion-Detection Model - Denning (IEEE Trans. Software Engineering, 1987)

elements.name: Secrets Management Service
elements.what: Credentials, keys, and tokens are held in a dedicated hardened service that issues them to workloads at runtime under authentication, audit, and rotation policies.
elements.problem: Secrets embedded in code, images, or config sprawl and leak; centralizing issuance gives one place for encryption at rest, access control, rotation, and audit.
elements.named_in: HashiCorp Vault Documentation (living); pattern also described in Kubernetes and cloud-provider secret-store documentation
elements.borderline: Named primarily in living vendor/platform documentation rather than a catalog work; kept because the component category is established across independent platforms and was parked by Phase 1's security scout.

elements.name: Federated Identity
elements.what: Authentication is delegated to a separate identity provider that the application trusts, receiving identity claims/tokens instead of managing credentials itself.
elements.problem: Per-application credential stores multiply attack surface and user friction; trusting an external identity authority centralizes authentication and enables single sign-on across systems.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (living)

elements.name: Secure Channel
elements.what: A connector type in which communication between components crosses an authenticated, encrypted transport so confidentiality and integrity hold over untrusted networks.
elements.problem: Data in transit over shared networks can be read and altered; making the channel itself cryptographically protected frees endpoints from trusting the path.
elements.named_in: Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering - Schumacher et al. (2006)

elements.name: Bulkhead (deployment partitioning)
elements.what: Capacity is partitioned into isolated pools - separate server groups, clusters, or instance sets per client, function, or criticality tier - so saturation or failure in one pool cannot sink the others.
elements.problem: Shared fleets let one abusive consumer or failing feature exhaust capacity for everyone; physical partitioning caps the blast radius at one compartment.
elements.named_in: Release It! - Nygard (2007/2018)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: design realm has bulkhead (in-process resource partitioning, e.g. per-feature thread pools); Nygard names both senses, and the deployment-level pool partitioning is the architecture sense. Kept per the same-name rule.

elements.name: N-Version Programming (system structure)
elements.what: N independently developed versions of a component execute in parallel on the same inputs and an adjudicator/voter selects the output, structuring the system for tolerance of design faults.
elements.problem: Replicating identical software tolerates only hardware faults - all copies share the same bugs; independently developed versions plus a voter make design faults outvotable.
elements.named_in: The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software - Avizienis (1985)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: design realm has n-version-programming (error-handling); Avizienis frames NVP explicitly as a fault-tolerant software architecture (versions + execution environment + adjudicator), which is this entry. Overlaps the RTDP Heterogeneous Redundancy pattern parked to the douglass/resilience scout - flag for merge-time dedup.

elements.name: Process Pairs
elements.what: A primary process executes while a backup process on another node receives checkpoints and takes over transparently when the primary fails.
elements.problem: Single-process services die with their host and lose in-flight state; a checkpointed backup converts host failure into a fast, state-preserving takeover.
elements.named_in: Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques - Gray & Reuter (1992); named earlier in Gray's 'Why Do Computers Stop' (1985)

elements.name: Crash-Only Software
elements.what: A system is structured so its components have exactly one stop method (crash) and one start method (recover), making crash-restart the universal, well-tested recovery path.
elements.problem: Separate clean-shutdown and crash-recovery code paths mean the rarely exercised one is broken when needed; designing for crash as the only stop makes recovery the routine path and enables microreboots of subcomponents.
elements.named_in: Crash-Only Software - Candea & Fox (HotOS IX, 2003)
elements.borderline: Same-name-two-realms: design realm's let-it-crash carries 'crash-only software' as an aka for the in-program supervisor/restart idiom; Candea-Fox's sense is a system-structure commitment (crash-only components, microrebootable architecture) and earns the architecture entry.

rejected.name: Twelve-Factor App
rejected.why: A methodology - a checklist of twelve practices for SaaS operability - not a structural element; its structural factors (external configuration, stateless processes, port binding, disposability) are covered by or bridgeable to specific elements. Charter judged as likely non-element; confirmed drop.

rejected.name: Packet Filter Firewall
rejected.why: Schumacher et al. catalog it as a separate pattern, but at catalog granularity it is a variant mechanism of the firewall choke point; kept as aka.

rejected.name: Proxy-Based Firewall
rejected.why: Same judgment as packet filter firewall - application-level variant of the firewall element; kept as aka.

rejected.name: Dark Launch
rejected.why: Deploying dark and exposing later is exactly the feature-flag-driven release structure; kept as aka.

rejected.name: Zero-Downtime Deployment
rejected.why: An umbrella goal-name, not a distinct mechanism; realized by blue-green, rolling, and canary structures already cataloged.

rejected.name: Infrastructure as Code
rejected.why: A practice (managing infrastructure through versioned definitions) - pass-7 process territory; its structural corollary is cataloged as immutable-infrastructure.

rejected.name: Reference Monitor (architecture twin)
rejected.why: Design realm already holds reference-monitor (robustness-security) with the PDP/PEP operational split in its aka; the system-level sense that the parked list demanded is the PDP/PEP externalized-authorization topology, cataloged here - a second reference-monitor node would duplicate it.

rejected.name: Compartmentalization
rejected.why: Parked as 'Defense in Depth / Compartmentalization'; the compartment structures are already specific entries (privilege-separation-arch, sandbox-architecture, bulkhead-arch, dmz) - a general compartmentalization node would be a catch-all, worthless for bridging.

rejected.name: GitOps
rejected.why: Met while judging deployment candidates: a delivery practice (declarative desired state reconciled from git), pass-7 territory, not a structural element.

rejected.name: Chaos Engineering
rejected.why: Met while judging operability candidates: an evaluation/verification method (like ATAM, methods are process, not elements).
